Print file preflight

Before you pay for a proof: check whether an export has the resolution for the size you mean to print, and compare up to five candidate masters head-to-head. Your artwork is read in this browser and never uploaded. Free, no signup.

Not sure what to aim for? What resolution do I need to print my artwork? has the pixel counts for every size below, at 150, 240 and 300 DPI. Already uploading to a print-on-demand service? See this tool vs. Printful.

Choose your print masters

Drop up to five JPEG or PNG files here

or

Name a file like harbor-11x14.jpg and it is checked at that print size. Nothing leaves your device.

Which master to print

Ranked at the target size above. A blocked file is never recommended, even when it has the most pixels.
#FilePixels DPI at targetCrop deltaStatus

Findings per file

FileRuleSeverityDetail

Take the record with you

The export states what was and was not checked, so the limitation travels with the file to your printer.

What this checks

RuleFloorSeverity
Implied DPIAt least 150 DPI at the named print sizeblocking
Pixel floorShort edge at least 1500px when no size is namedblocking
FormatJPEG or PNGblocking
File sizeAt most 50 MiBblocking
Web filenameNo web, thumbnail, lowres, instagram, facebookblocking
Named cropAspect within 4% of the named sizereview

What this does not check

This reads dimensions, byte size, format and filename. It is blind to everything that actually decides how a print looks:

  • Colour. No profile inspection, no gamut check, no soft proof. A file can pass here and print with a colour cast.
  • Sharpness and noise. An upscaled or heavily denoised file has the pixel count without the detail, and nothing here can tell the difference.
  • Paper, press and finish. The same file on matte, glossy and canvas is three different results, and each lab has its own requirements.

So clearing the floor means the file is not obviously too small — nothing more. Order a proof.

Questions

What DPI does a print master need?

This tool checks a documented floor of 150 DPI at the print size named in the filename. That is a conservative floor for fine-art and photographic printing rather than an ideal: many labs prefer 240 or 300 DPI, and some accept less for large pieces viewed from a distance. Implied DPI is simply your pixel dimensions divided by the physical print size, so the same file is print-ready at 8x10 and far below the floor at 24x36.

How does the tool know what size I am printing?

It reads a size token out of the filename. A file called harbor-11x14.jpg is checked as an 11x14 print, and the named size is matched in either orientation, so a landscape file is measured against 14x11. If no supported size appears in the filename, the tool falls back to a conservative floor of 1500 pixels on the short edge instead of guessing a print size. The compare view lets you pick any supported size explicitly.

Why does the tool block a file for its filename?

Filenames containing web, thumbnail, lowres, instagram, or facebook are almost always a web export that was resized and recompressed for a screen. Such a file can still have enough pixels to clear the DPI floor, which is exactly why it is worth flagging: the resolution looks fine while the file has already lost the detail a print needs. It is a filename convention check, so rename the file if it is genuinely your print master.

Is my artwork uploaded anywhere?

No. The files are opened by your own browser to read their pixel dimensions, and nothing is transmitted. There is no server, no account, and no upload step. You can disconnect from the network and the tool still works.

Does a passing preflight mean my print will look good?

No. This is limited automated evidence, not a print-ready warranty or lab approval. It reads dimensions, byte size, format and filename — it cannot judge colour accuracy, sharpness, noise, colour profile, paper choice, or how a specific press and stock will render your image. Order a proof and confirm requirements with your printer before committing to a run.

Disclaimer

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not printing, production, colour-management, or professional advice, and it does not replace a qualified printer or colour manager. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Privacy

Everything runs in your browser. Your artwork is never uploaded, and we don't have accounts, tracking cookies, or an analytics vendor. This page counts anonymous, local feature-use events (e.g. "files were compared") in your own browser's localStorage — never filenames, images, or anything identifying — only to help this project's maintainers tell whether the tool is used at all. Nothing is sent anywhere.

← Print file preflight — free DPI and print-size checker

This tool vs. Printful

Two different shapes: Printful is account-based print-on-demand fulfillment for running a print storefront. This page is a free, private check of one file's resolution and filename before you upload it anywhere.

What each is for

Printful is a print-on-demand and warehousing company, founded in 2013, that lets a seller upload artwork, connect it to an online store — Shopify, Etsy, WooCommerce and others — and have each order printed and shipped only after a customer buys it, so the seller holds no inventory. It is used through a free account, with production and shipping charged per order rather than a flat subscription. Printful's own upload dashboard runs its own checks on a file after you submit it, and this page does not restate its current published resolution guidance or pricing, because printful.com is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact wording: only its well-documented identity and category — print-on-demand fulfillment, connected to a seller's own storefront — are stated here.

This tool does none of what Printful does. It does not host a storefront, print anything, or ship anything. It reads a candidate file's pixel dimensions, format, byte size, and filename directly in your browser, checks the implied DPI at the print size named in the filename against a documented 150 DPI floor, ranks up to five candidate masters head-to-head at one target size, and exports a dated technical record — all before the file is ever uploaded anywhere. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and never transmits the artwork.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I want to sell prints through a connected storefront, with fulfillment, shipping, and payment handled for me.Printful, or a comparable print-on-demand service — running a store is not something this tool does.
Is this specific export sharp enough to print at the size I plan to sell it?This tool's implied-DPI check, before you upload anywhere.
I have several exports of the same image and need to know which one to submit.This tool's five-way ranked comparison.
I already got a low-resolution warning after uploading to a POD platform — could I have caught it sooner?Yes: this tool checks the same kind of resolution problem before any upload, at no cost and with no account.
Do I need an account or a connected store to check a file?This tool: no. Printful: yes, an account and a connected store.
Is my artwork sent anywhere to be checked?This tool: no, it never leaves your device. Printful: yes — uploading the file is the point, since it is what gets printed.
What resolution do I actually need for a given print size?This tool's own resolution walkthrough.

Most artists get different value from each: Printful (or a comparable print-on-demand service) for running an actual storefront with fulfillment and shipping handled per order, and a private check like this one for an instant, no-account answer to whether one candidate file is sharp enough before any of it touches a platform. This page's own result is a resolution and filename check, not a colour proof, a print approval, or a substitute for whatever validation Printful or any other print-on-demand service runs on its own upload.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, every check runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this tool or Printful?

They do different jobs, and an artist selling prints will likely use both. Printful is a print-on-demand and warehousing company, founded in 2013, that lets a seller upload artwork, connect it to an online store (Shopify, Etsy, WooCommerce and others), and have each order printed and shipped only after a customer buys it — so the seller holds no inventory. It is used through a free account, with production and shipping charged per order. Printful's own upload dashboard runs its own checks on a file after you submit it, and its current published thresholds are not restated here because this session cannot reach printful.com to confirm today's exact wording. This tool does one narrower thing: it reads a candidate file's pixel dimensions, format, byte size, and filename in your own browser, checks the implied DPI at the print size named in the filename against a documented 150 DPI floor, ranks up to five candidates head-to-head, and exports a dated technical record — all before the file is ever uploaded anywhere. It runs free, keeps no account, and never transmits the artwork. An artist who wants to sell through a connected storefront with fulfillment, shipping, and payment handled for them is better served by Printful or a comparable print-on-demand service; an artist who wants to know, in seconds and before any upload, whether a specific export is sharp enough for a specific size is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with Printful?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Printful. Printful is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this tool is and is not.

what-resolution-do-i-need-to-print-my-ar.text:
← Print file preflight — free DPI and print-size checker

What resolution do I need to print my artwork?

There is no answer that is a single number, and that is the whole difficulty. Print resolution is a ratio between the pixels you have and the inches you are spreading them across — so the same file is comfortably print-ready at one size and obviously short at another.

Check your own file — free, nothing is uploaded

The one piece of arithmetic

Implied DPI = pixels ÷ inches. A master that is 2400 × 3000 pixels is 300 DPI printed at 8×10, 150 DPI at 16×20, and 100 DPI at 24×30. Nothing about the file changed; only the sheet did.

Turn that around and you get the number you actually want when you are preparing a master: pixels needed = inches × target DPI. Decide the biggest size you intend to sell, pick the DPI your printer works to, and multiply.

Pixels needed, size by size

These are the seven sizes the checker on this site knows, at three common targets. 150 DPI is the floor it enforces; 240 and 300 are what many labs prefer for work viewed close up.

Print size150 DPI (floor)240 DPI300 DPI
5×7 in750 × 1050 px1200 × 1680 px1500 × 2100 px
8×10 in1200 × 1500 px1920 × 2400 px2400 × 3000 px
11×14 in1650 × 2100 px2640 × 3360 px3300 × 4200 px
12×16 in1800 × 2400 px2880 × 3840 px3600 × 4800 px
16×20 in2400 × 3000 px3840 × 4800 px4800 × 6000 px
18×24 in2700 × 3600 px4320 × 5760 px5400 × 7200 px
24×36 in3600 × 5400 px5760 × 8640 px7200 × 10800 px

Worth noticing at the bottom of that table: a 24×36 at 300 DPI is about 78 megapixels. Very few single camera frames reach it, which is why large-format work is routinely printed nearer the floor than the ideal, and why a floor is a more useful test than an aspiration.

What the number does not tell you

Clearing a DPI floor means the file has enough pixels. It does not mean the print will be good.

  • A web export can pass on pixels and still be wrong. A file resized and recompressed for a screen has already thrown away detail; the remaining pixels are soft even though there are enough of them. That is why the checker flags filenames containing web, thumbnail, lowres, instagram or facebook separately from the DPI test.
  • The stored DPI field is not the resolution. The number saved in a JPEG or TIFF header is a suggested print size and carries no pixels with it. Changing it from 72 to 300 without resampling leaves the file byte-for-byte as capable as it was.
  • Aspect ratio decides what gets cropped. A 4:3 capture printed at 11×14 loses something from an edge. Deciding what, rather than letting the lab decide, is part of preparing a master.
  • Colour, paper and profile are a different problem entirely. No pixel count predicts how a particular ink and paper will render your blacks. That is what a proof is for.

If the file is too small

Upscaling raises the pixel count without recovering detail that was never captured, so it changes what a preflight check reports without changing what the print looks like. Current upscalers can make an enlargement acceptable, particularly on textured or painterly work, but they are inventing plausible detail rather than restoring real detail. The honest options are to print smaller, to rescan or rephotograph the original at higher resolution, or to go ahead knowingly — after a proof, not instead of one.

Check a file before you pay for a proof

Drop in up to five candidate masters, pick the size you are printing, and see the implied DPI for each, which ones clear the floor, and which one is the best of what you have. It runs entirely in your browser — your artwork is never uploaded, and there is no account.

Open the free print file preflight

Common questions

What resolution do I need to print my artwork?

It depends entirely on how big the print is, because resolution for print is a ratio rather than a property of the file. Implied DPI is your pixel dimensions divided by the physical print size in inches, so a 2400 by 3000 pixel file is 300 DPI at 8x10 and 100 DPI at 24x30. There is no such thing as a file that is high resolution in the abstract. Decide the largest size you intend to sell, divide the pixels by the inches, and check that the number clears the floor your printer works to.

How many pixels do I need for a 16x20 print?

Multiply each dimension in inches by the DPI you are targeting. At 150 DPI a 16x20 needs 2400 by 3000 pixels, at 240 DPI it needs 3840 by 4800, and at 300 DPI it needs 4800 by 6000. The same arithmetic gives you any other size: an 11x14 at 300 DPI is 3300 by 4200 pixels, and a 24x36 at 300 DPI is 7200 by 10800, which is about 78 megapixels and beyond a single frame from most cameras.

Is 150 DPI good enough for a print?

It is a floor rather than a target. The preflight tool on this site checks 150 DPI at the named print size because below that the loss of detail is visible at any normal viewing distance, and because a file that fails a conservative floor certainly fails a strict one. Many labs prefer 240 or 300 DPI for work viewed close up, and some accept less than 150 for large pieces meant to be seen from across a room. Ask the printer you actually intend to use, and treat 150 as the point below which the answer is definitely no.

Can I just upscale the file to reach the DPI I need?

Resampling raises the pixel count and does not recover detail that was never captured, so it changes the number a preflight check reports without changing what the print will look like. Modern upscalers can make an enlargement look acceptable, especially on textured or painterly work, but they are inventing plausible detail rather than restoring real detail. If the master is genuinely short of pixels, the honest options are to print smaller, rescan or rephotograph the original at a higher resolution, or accept the enlargement knowingly after seeing a proof.

Does the DPI setting saved in the file matter?

Not for whether the file is big enough. The DPI field stored in a JPEG or TIFF header is only a suggested print size; it carries no pixels with it, and changing it from 72 to 300 in an image editor without resampling leaves the file identical. What matters is the pixel dimensions and the inches you are printing them across. That is why the checker on this site reads the actual decoded width and height rather than trusting the metadata.

Why does my file pass at one size and fail at another?

Because the pixel count is fixed and the inches are not. Spreading the same pixels over a larger sheet lowers the implied DPI in direct proportion, so a master that comfortably clears a floor at 8x10 can be less than half of it at 16x20 and a quarter of it at 24x30. This is the most common surprise for an artist listing one file at several sizes, and it is why it is worth checking against the largest size you plan to offer rather than the smallest.
